paragraphs: The paper asks how to predict revenue from a particular assortment when information about consumer preferences is limited. The available evidence might describe individual preference relationships without revealing a complete picture of how everyone chooses. The challenge is to connect those partial observations to the financial consequences of offering a specific collection of alternatives.

The authors represent consumer choice through a distribution over preference lists. A preference list describes an ordering of alternatives, while the distribution allows different consumers to have different orderings. This gives the framework a broad way to describe variation in choice. Its central task is to use limited decision data within that representation to answer questions about assortment revenue.

The contribution is a framework together with several algorithms designed to be tractable in both their data requirements and computation. This matters because a flexible description of preferences is useful for decision-making only if it can support calculations from the information actually available. The paper positions this problem across operations research, marketing, and econometrics.
neurips-2009-a-data-driven-approach-to-m.tldr: The paper develops tractable algorithms for predicting assortment revenue from limited choice data using distributions over consumer preference lists.

paragraphs: The paper studies what happens when a family of probability distributions is mapped through a linear projection. The families have specified first and second moments, which constrain their averages and variation. The main result says these projections are surjective: every distribution in the corresponding projected family can be obtained from a distribution in the original family, regardless of dimension.

This property matters for worst-case analysis because it establishes that working with the projected family does not introduce unattainable possibilities. The authors also extend their result to families with additional shape restrictions, including symmetry, unimodality, and log-concavity. These extensions allow the projection argument to apply when the available knowledge goes beyond moments alone.

Combining the projection results with established inequalities for single-variable distributions yields new worst-case analyses of risk criteria. One stated consequence concerns portfolio selection: optimizing worst-case value-at-risk and worst-case conditional value-at-risk produces identical portfolios in the setting considered. The equivalence concerns the resulting portfolio choices under these worst-case criteria, rather than asserting that the two risk measures are interchangeable in general.
neurips-2009-a-general-projection-proper.tldr: A projection theorem for moment-constrained distribution families enables worst-case risk analyses, including an equivalence between two portfolio-selection criteria.

paragraphs: The paper addresses separating overlapping sounds from a recording with only one audio channel. Its setting includes training examples of the kinds of sounds present in the mixture. Those examples provide information about the sources that the algorithm is trying to recover, making this a problem of separating known sound types.

The main design choice is how to use that training material. Instead of compressing each sound type into a compact statistical model, the method uses the training data itself as the source representation. It describes a mixture through a sparse combination of those examples, meaning that relatively few parts of the available representation contribute to a particular explanation of the mixture.

The authors show that this sparse representation can describe mixtures of known sounds and report significantly better separation than similar systems using compact statistical models. The result supports retaining detailed training examples as a useful modeling choice for this task. Its practical significance is that reducing a sound collection to a compact model is not the only effective route to separating its contributions.
neurips-2009-a-sparse-non-parametric-app.tldr: Representing known sound mixtures as sparse combinations of training examples improves single-channel separation over similar compact statistical models.

paragraphs: Some categories are defined more naturally by relationships among their parts than by a list of features. The paper studies how such relational categories can be learned and used. Its central proposal is that learners acquire abstract schemata: representations of the relational structure that members of a category have in common.

The authors develop a hierarchical generative model built around this idea. The hierarchy provides a framework for learning category-level relational patterns rather than placing the main explanatory burden on comparisons between concrete examples. The distinction concerns what supports generalization: an abstract representation of shared relationships can serve as the basis for recognizing or reasoning about category members.

Two experiments examine this account. The first suggests that an abstraction-based model can handle some tasks previously used as evidence for comparison-based explanations. The second addresses learning a schema from a single example, which challenges comparison-based approaches but fits naturally within the proposed account. Together, the experiments support abstraction as an explanation of these learning abilities without establishing that comparison plays no role.
neurips-2009-abstraction-and-relational-.tldr: A hierarchical generative model explains relational learning through abstract schemata and naturally accommodates learning a schema from one example.

paragraphs: The paper develops faster ways to infer the structure of non-decomposable Gaussian graphical models using approximate Bayesian methods. The computational task involves evaluating candidate graphs and generating promising structures. The authors address both parts, so improvements in scoring can be combined with improvements in how candidates are proposed.

First, they use convex precision-matrix estimation to efficiently calculate BIC or Laplace approximations to a graph's marginal likelihood. These approximations provide fast scores for stochastic local search. Second, their Neighborhood Fusion method generates graph candidates without local search by using sparse regression to sample candidate Markov blankets, or local dependency neighborhoods, for individual nodes. A hybrid method combines Neighborhood Fusion with stochastic local search.

Experiments assess both recovery of graph structure and prediction on synthetic and real-world data. Under realistic computational limits, Neighborhood Fusion and the hybrid outperform the compared state-of-the-art local search methods. The finding emphasizes the value of generating useful graph proposals efficiently: within a limited computation budget, the search strategy matters alongside the quality of the scoring function.
neurips-2009-accelerating-bayesian-struc.tldr: Faster graph scoring and Neighborhood Fusion proposals improve approximate Bayesian graph inference under realistic computational budgets.

paragraphs: The paper proposes an anomaly detector that learns from examples of nominal, or ordinary, behavior. It constructs nearest-neighbor graphs from these examples and derives a score for a new observation. A test sample is declared anomalous when its score falls below a threshold q, intended to represent the desired false-alarm level.

The method is non-parametric and can adapt to local structure, including changes in local dimensionality. It does not require selecting complicated tuning parameters or a class of functions for approximation. Its computational cost grows linearly with the number of dimensions and quadratically with the number of nominal examples, making these two aspects of scale affect the workload differently.

The theoretical guarantee is asymptotic and assumes the anomaly density is a mixture of the nominal density and a known density. In that setting, the detector is uniformly most powerful at the specified false-alarm level. The authors also demonstrate it on artificial and real high-dimensional datasets. The guarantee therefore supplies a precise conditional foundation for a detector that is also examined empirically.
neurips-2009-anomaly-detection-with-scor.tldr: Nearest-neighbor graph scores enable adaptive anomaly detection with an asymptotic optimality guarantee under a specified anomaly-mixture model.

paragraphs: The paper brings directed acyclic graphs and factor models into a common Bayesian learning framework. These provide different ways to describe relationships among variables, and the authors also want to compare them within the same approach. Their starting point is a connection between the two model families that supports shared machinery for inference.

The framework assigns distinct roles to several modeling choices. Spike-and-slab priors encourage sparse structures, helping determine which relationships should be present. Heavy-tailed priors provide identifiability, which the authors require to obtain variable orderings that lead to valid directed acyclic graphs. Predictive densities then supply the basis for comparing the models.

This combination makes structure learning and model comparison parts of one procedure rather than disconnected decisions. Sparsity concerns the relationships retained, while identifiability supports the ordering needed for a valid graph. Experiments on artificial and biological data demonstrate the approach's effectiveness and report better performance than several state-of-the-art methods. Those results provide empirical support for the framework across the two kinds of data examined.
neurips-2009-bayesian-sparse-factor-mode.tldr: A shared Bayesian framework learns sparse factor models and directed acyclic graphs and compares them through predictive densities.

paragraphs: The paper tackles choosing among linear estimators for non-parametric regression. This includes selecting a linear regression model, setting the strength of regularization in kernel ridge regression or spline smoothing, and choosing a kernel in multiple kernel learning. These decisions all require a way to calibrate the competing estimators from data.

The proposed algorithm first estimates the noise variance using the idea of a minimal penalty. The authors prove that this estimate is consistent. They then insert it into Mallows' C_L penalty to choose an estimator. This separates the calibration into estimating the amount of noise and using that estimate to guide the final selection.

The resulting selection procedure satisfies an oracle inequality, a theoretical comparison with the performance of a best candidate reference. Simulations involving kernel ridge regression and multiple kernel learning show that the method often improves significantly on existing procedures, including ten-fold and generalized cross-validation. The contribution combines a theoretical justification for data-driven calibration with empirical evidence of gains in the tested settings.
neurips-2009-data-driven-calibration-of-.tldr: Estimating noise through minimal penalties yields a theoretically justified estimator-selection procedure that often improves on cross-validation in simulations.

paragraphs: Kernel methods can become difficult to scale because they rely on a matrix of relationships among data points. A low-rank approximation replaces that matrix with a more compact representation. The paper develops ensemble Nystrom algorithms, which combine multiple Nystrom approximations to improve the accuracy of this representation.

The authors study several ways to form the ensemble. These include simple averaging, exponential weighting, and regression-based combinations. The shared idea is to use a mixture of approximations instead of relying on a single standard Nystrom approximation. Comparing these variants examines how the choice of combination method contributes to the resulting matrix approximation.

The paper supports the approach with both theoretical analysis and experiments. Its error bounds guarantee a better convergence rate than the standard Nystrom method, and evaluations on datasets with up to one million points show significant performance improvements over that method. These findings matter because low-rank approximation is a central tool for extending kernel methods to very large datasets, and the ensemble improves the approximation at the heart of that strategy.
neurips-2009-ensemble-nystrom-method-37e.tldr: Combining Nystrom approximations improves low-rank kernel approximation, with stronger convergence guarantees and empirical gains on datasets up to one million points.

paragraphs: Learning to detect many object categories raises a tradeoff between specialized detectors and representations shared across classes. Specialized detectors tend to perform well, while sharing can reduce inference time but complicate training. Learning categories sequentially offers another option: transfer existing knowledge to new classes to shorten training, with possible dependence on learning order and incomplete use of shared structure.

The paper implements three strategies within one generative hierarchical framework: training categories independently, training them jointly, and learning them sequentially. A common framework makes it possible to examine these learning choices together. The study focuses particularly on what happens as the number of learned object classes increases.

The authors evaluate detection performance alongside computational requirements, covering both space and time on several recognition datasets. The contribution is a systematic experimental comparison of the three strategies in a hierarchical setting. It makes the relevant decision broader than detection accuracy alone: a strategy must also be assessed by how its training, inference, and storage behavior develop as more categories are introduced.
neurips-2009-evaluating-multi-class-lear.tldr: The paper compares independent, joint, and sequential object-category learning within one hierarchical framework as the number of classes grows.

paragraphs: The paper addresses a computational bottleneck in kernel learning for nonlinear data modeling. Problems such as Maximum Variance Unfolding and Pairwise Constraint Propagation can be expressed as semidefinite programs. Although this formulation has favorable theoretical solvability properties, processing its large matrix inequality constraints can make numerical computation impractical at scale.

The authors show that a large class of kernel-learning problems can instead be expressed as semidefinite-quadratic-linear programs. The reformulation contains a simple positive semidefinite constraint, a second-order cone constraint, and linear constraints. The key contribution is a change in the form of the optimization problem that makes its constraints easier to handle numerically.

The stated speedup over earlier approaches is at least on the order of m to the power 2.5, where m denotes the matrix dimension. Experiments also demonstrate strong computational efficiency. The result shows why the specific mathematical representation of a learning problem matters: two formulations aimed at the same task can impose very different numerical workloads, especially as their matrices grow.
neurips-2009-fast-graph-laplacian-regula.tldr: Reformulating a large class of kernel-learning problems with simpler constraints yields substantial computational speedups over previous semidefinite approaches.

paragraphs: The paper studies learning when observations are dependent rather than independent and identically distributed. Its setting is alpha-mixing processes, a class that places conditions on how statistical dependence behaves. The aim is to establish learning guarantees that account for this dependence instead of relying directly on an independence assumption.

The main result is an oracle inequality for generic regularized empirical risk minimization algorithms. Such algorithms balance fit to the observed data against a regularization penalty. An oracle inequality provides a way to compare their performance with an ideal reference choice. The authors use this result to derive learning rates for particular methods, including least-squares support vector machines.

The proof adapts localization ideas developed for independent observations to the dependent setting. The resulting learning rates are close to the optimal rates known for independent and identically distributed data. This indicates that, for the processes and methods covered by the analysis, dependence can be accommodated while retaining strong rates of learning. The conclusion is tied to the alpha-mixing setting rather than arbitrary dependence.
neurips-2009-fast-learning-from-non-i-i-.tldr: An oracle inequality gives regularized learning methods rates close to optimal independent-data rates when observations come from alpha-mixing processes.

paragraphs: Combining fMRI measurements across people requires a way to match corresponding cortical locations. This alignment matters for the statistical power of group analyses. The paper proposes finding correspondence through functional connectivity, using patterns of functional relationships across the cortex as the information that guides alignment.

The algorithm works across multiple subjects and aligns spatial patterns of connectivity. Its organizing principle differs from alignment based on anatomy: correspondence is derived from how cortical locations participate in functional patterns. This provides a way to match subjects according to the functional organization represented in their fMRI data.

The authors test the method using measurements collected while participants view a movie. They then cross-validate the learned correspondence on a second movie dataset that was not used to construct the alignment. The correspondence successfully generalizes to that separate dataset. This finding matters because it shows that the alignment captures functional relationships that remain useful beyond the particular movie measurements from which it was derived.
neurips-2009-fmri-based-inter-subject-co.tldr: Aligning subjects through functional connectivity produces cortical correspondences that generalize to a separate movie-viewing fMRI dataset.

paragraphs: The paper examines how classifiers can use information distributed across functional brain regions. Many multi-voxel analysis approaches either combine regions into one uniform collection or analyze them independently. Both choices leave out explicit interactions among regions, even though those interactions can matter for processing information during a task.

The authors use a hidden conditional random field to connect classifiers associated with regions of interest. Each regional classifier makes predictions using both its own voxel measurements and predictions from connected regional classifiers. They also introduce a structure-learning method that discovers the connections automatically within the same framework.

Experiments use fMRI data collected while people view natural-scene images. The model improves prediction accuracy both for individual regions and for the top-level classifier that combines their information, while uncovering some meaningful connections. These results support treating regional predictions as interdependent. The learned connections provide an additional view of how information from different regions contributes to the classification task alongside the gains in predictive performance.
neurips-2009-hierarchical-mixture-of-cla.tldr: Connecting regional fMRI classifiers in a learned graphical structure improves predictions and reveals meaningful relationships among brain regions.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to represent continuous changes in images. It treats these changes as movement along a smooth nonlinear manifold and learns transformation operators that describe that movement. The application is modeling how natural images vary over time and scale, with the transformations themselves serving as a representation of change.

The operators are expressed through a basis adapted to the statistics of the data. A particular trajectory of measurements has an infinitesimal generator, which specifies its local continuous transformation. The method represents that generator as a linear combination of only a few basis elements. This gives the learned representation a compact way to describe the transformations associated with a trajectory.

The authors illustrate how these operators can support efficient coding of time-varying images. Instead of describing temporal and scale changes only through the resulting images, the representation describes them in terms of learned transformations. The contribution connects the geometry of continuous image variation with a data-adapted set of operators that can be combined economically.
neurips-2009-learning-transport-operator.tldr: The method learns continuous image transformations whose generators use few basis elements, supporting efficient descriptions of changes over time and scale.

paragraphs: The paper seeks binary representations of high-dimensional vectors that preserve useful similarity information. Similar vectors should receive similar strings of bits, so comparing the codes reflects relationships in the original space. The relevant code comparison is Hamming distance: the number of bit positions at which two strings differ.

The authors introduce a distribution-free encoding scheme based on random projections. Its central property links the expected Hamming distance between two codes to a shift-invariant kernel value for the original vectors, such as a Gaussian kernel. This makes the connection between binary similarity and the chosen kernel explicit, with the stated relationship expressed as an expectation over the randomized encoding.

The paper provides a theoretical analysis of convergence and reports favorable experimental performance compared with spectral hashing. The analysis supports understanding how the randomized codes behave, while the experiments examine their practical performance against an existing method. Together, these contributions establish a simple route from kernel-based similarity to binary representations without requiring a specified distribution for the data.
neurips-2009-locality-sensitive-binary-c.tldr: Random projections produce binary codes whose expected Hamming distances relate to shift-invariant kernel similarities, with theory and favorable empirical comparisons.

paragraphs: The paper studies control when the underlying state is nonlinear, noisy, continuous, and only partly observable. Such systems may also be difficult to explore and poorly described by first principles. The authors investigate manifold embeddings as reconstructed observable states for an offline, model-based reinforcement-learning approach.

The embedding supplies the state representation used for learning control. The authors show that a system's embedding changes as learning proceeds and that the best-performing embeddings represent the dynamics of both the uncontrolled system and the system under adaptive control. This makes the representation of controlled behavior an important part of reconstructing a useful state space.

The application is neurostimulation for epilepsy. In simulation, the approach learns a stimulation policy that treats epilepsy more efficiently than conventional policies. The learned policy is then tested in real-world experiments on animal brain slices, where it completely suppresses seizures in those experiments. These results connect the state-reconstruction approach to a demonstrated control outcome, with the experimental seizure-suppression claim specifically grounded in the brain-slice setting.
neurips-2009-manifold-embeddings-for-mod.tldr: Manifold-based state reconstruction supports learning a neurostimulation policy that improves simulated treatment efficiency and suppresses seizures in animal brain-slice experiments.

paragraphs: The paper adds manifold regularization to Sliced Inverse Regression, or SIR. Its purpose is to make the method account for the local geometry of the data when finding projection directions. Nearby relationships among observations therefore become part of the information used to determine the resulting representation.

The regularization is based on a graph Laplacian. Beyond incorporating geometry, the authors show that it enables SIR to handle transductive and semi-supervised learning problems. These settings broaden the role of the available data beyond fully labeled training examples. The projection directions are optimized with a conjugate-gradient method on the Grassmann manifold, a geometric space for representing subspaces.

The theoretical contribution is a root-n convergence result for the proposed graph-Laplacian regularization. The authors also report experimental results that support their theory. The work thus combines a statistical guarantee with an optimization method for the regularized projections. Its significance is that local data geometry becomes usable within SIR while retaining a stated convergence rate and extending the learning settings it can address.
neurips-2009-manifold-regularization-for.tldr: Graph-Laplacian regularization adds local geometry and semi-supervised capabilities to SIR, with a proven root-n convergence rate.

paragraphs: Object detection and image segmentation describe related aspects of a scene: which objects are present and how the image is divided into labeled parts. The paper argues that the tasks can benefit from exchanging information. Separate representations, however, make joint reasoning awkward and can leave the interpretation of scene parts ambiguous.

The authors propose a hierarchical, region-based probabilistic model that reasons jointly about pixels, regions, and objects. These levels form one description of the scene. Every pixel is accounted for, and global consistency is enforced among the model's variables. This provides a shared structure through which object-level and region-level information can influence the interpretation of the image.

Experiments on challenging vision datasets show a significant improvement over state-of-the-art object detection accuracy. The stated finding supports the value of combining the tasks within a coherent scene model. The approach matters because information sharing is built into the representation itself: decisions about objects and image regions are required to fit together as parts of a single explanation.
neurips-2009-region-based-segmentation-a.tldr: A unified probabilistic model of pixels, regions, and objects jointly handles segmentation and detection and improves object detection accuracy.

paragraphs: Distance metric learning aims to learn how distances between examples should be measured for a task. The paper examines the generalization error of regularized metric learning: how well a learned distance rule performs beyond the data used to fit it. The central concern is whether high dimensionality must worsen the theoretical guarantee.

The authors show that, with appropriate constraints, the generalization error could be independent of dimensionality. This is a conditional result: the constraints are part of what makes dimension independence possible. It provides theoretical motivation for using regularized metric learning on high-dimensional data, where a guarantee that grows with dimension could become less useful.

The paper also introduces an efficient online learning algorithm and evaluates it on classification and face recognition. The empirical studies find it effective relative to state-of-the-art metric-learning methods and efficient and robust on high-dimensional data. The contribution therefore connects a conditional statistical result with an algorithm whose practical behavior is assessed on tasks that use learned distances.
neurips-2009-regularized-distance-metric.tldr: Appropriate constraints can make regularized metric-learning generalization independent of dimension, and an online algorithm performs effectively on high-dimensional tasks.

paragraphs: The paper investigates how spike-timing-dependent plasticity, or STDP, could give spiking neural circuits a useful computational function. The proposed setting combines STDP with a stochastic soft winner-take-all circuit. Within that combination, neurons develop synaptic weights that implicitly model subclasses, described as hidden causes, of high-dimensional input spike patterns.

After learning, a neuron fires when the current input best matches its internal model. The authors suggest that such circuits could reduce the dimensionality of incoming information while autonomously constructing models of the probability distributions behind their inputs. This interpretation links the behavior of individual neurons to a statistical description of patterns across hundreds of presynaptic neurons.

The authors provide a mathematical account of how this function can arise and be maintained. In particular, they show that STDP can approximate a stochastic online expectation-maximization algorithm for modeling the input data. They also establish a corresponding result for Hebbian learning in artificial neural networks. The work offers a principled computational interpretation of the specified learning-and-circuit combination.
neurips-2009-stdp-enables-spiking-neuron.tldr: STDP in stochastic soft winner-take-all circuits approximates online expectation-maximization, enabling neurons to learn implicit models of input-pattern subclasses.

paragraphs: The paper addresses maximizing a submodular set function while limiting how many items can be selected. This formulation appears in applications such as feature selection and active learning. The optimization problem is NP-hard, motivating methods that can pursue exact solutions while also reporting how good an unfinished solution is.

The proposed algorithm uses a cutting-plane approach implemented through repeated small binary-integer linear programs. It is guaranteed to reach an exact solution after finitely many iterations, and the authors report fast convergence in practice. This is an exact optimization method whose finite-termination guarantee does not amount to a polynomial-time guarantee.

A complementary procedure supplies decreasing upper bounds on the optimal objective value, while the main algorithm supplies increasing lower bounds. The gap between them indicates the remaining uncertainty about solution quality. This allows computation to stop once a desired tolerance is met, rather than always waiting for exact completion. Evaluations on sensor placement and feature selection show good performance, illustrating the value of combining exact search with usable progress certificates.
neurips-2009-submodularity-cuts-and-appl.tldr: A cutting-plane algorithm exactly solves cardinality-constrained submodular maximization and provides bounds that support early stopping at a chosen tolerance.

paragraphs: The paper models systems whose directed dependency structures change over time. A fixed network can miss this rewiring when biological or neural systems undergo dynamic transformations. The authors propose time-varying dynamic Bayesian networks to represent changing relationships in non-stationary time series, where limited observations make structure learning especially challenging.

Their learning procedure combines autoregression with kernel reweighting and an l1 regularization penalty. These components support estimating temporal relationships while encouraging sparse network structures. The resulting model allows the pattern of directed dependencies itself to vary, rather than treating every part of the time series as governed by one unchanging graph.

The authors establish computational efficiency and provable asymptotic consistency for their approach. They apply it to measurements from the yeast cell cycle and brain responses to visual stimuli, revealing dynamics in both systems. The contribution is a framework for studying changes in relationships among measured variables, with theoretical support for estimation and applications showing what a changing network representation can expose.
neurips-2009-time-varying-dynamic-bayesi.tldr: Time-varying dynamic Bayesian networks learn changing directed dependencies in biological and neural time series using an efficient, asymptotically consistent procedure.

paragraphs: The paper seeks likely object regions in cluttered web images without using labels. Its method alternates between choosing a small set of strong reference regions across the dataset and refining candidate regions in each image using those references. The references and localizations are therefore improved through repeated interaction.

Both steps are expressed as ranking problems on similarity networks of proposed regions. Link analysis ranks the hypotheses in two different networks, supporting exemplar selection in one step and region refinement in the other. This gives the alternating procedure a shared computational basis while allowing the two steps to serve different roles.

On PASCAL 06, the method's unsupervised localization performance exceeds one state-of-the-art technique and is comparable to supervised methods. The authors also test scalability using five objects in a Flickr dataset containing more than 200,000 images. These results support the approach as a fast, scalable way to find object regions through similarities across an image collection, with the reported comparisons tied to the evaluated datasets.
neurips-2009-unsupervised-detection-of-r.tldr: Alternating link-based rankings of reference regions and image hypotheses localize objects without labels and scale to a large web-image collection.

paragraphs: The paper investigates whether hierarchical representations learned from unlabeled data are useful for audio recognition. It applies convolutional deep belief networks to audio and evaluates the resulting representations on several classification tasks. The focus is on learning useful features from the recordings before assessing them through classification.

For speech, the authors find that learned features correspond to phones or phonemes, units associated with speech sounds. This gives the representation a meaningful connection to the structure of the input. It shows that learning from unlabeled audio can produce features aligned with recognizable speech units in the studied setting.

The learned representations also achieve very good performance across multiple audio classification tasks. Together, the feature correspondence and classification results provide empirical support for applying this kind of deep learning to auditory data. The contribution is both a demonstration of useful learned audio structure and an evaluation of its predictive value, motivating broader investigation of hierarchical feature learning for audio recognition.
neurips-2009-unsupervised-feature-learni.tldr: Convolutional deep belief networks learn useful features from unlabeled audio, including speech-sound representations, and perform well across multiple classification tasks.
